questions.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Such that the Limit of a Piecewise Function Exists
questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x),$ defined as follows:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x, & x\le 1 \\ x+a, & 1<x<3 \\ {x}^{2}-2x, & x\ge 3\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

It is known that $f$ is continuous at $x=1.$ Find the value of $a.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $a=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)$ exists.

In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left- and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

* Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}({e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x) \\  & ={e}^{1}+{1}^{2}+1 \\  & =e+2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

* Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=x+a.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(x+a) \\  & =1+a.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ 1+a & =e+2 \\ a & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x),$ defined as follows:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x, & x\le 1 \\ x+a, & 1<x<3 \\ {x}^{2}-2x, & x\ge 3\end{aligned}
$$

Earlier part 1:

It is known that $f$ is continuous at $x=1.$ Find the value of $a.$

                                        $e+1$

Current part:

${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{x}^{3}+2}{f(x)}=$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
In part 1, we found that ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)=e+2\ne 0.$

Applying the quotient rule for limits, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{x}^{3}+2}{f(x)} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}{x}^{3}+2}{{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{3}+2}{e+2} \\  & =\frac{3}{e+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Interval Over Which the Average Rate of Change of a Function is a Given Number
questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x),$ defined as follows:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}+{x}^{2}+x, & x\le 1 \\ x+a, & 1<x<3 \\ {x}^{2}-2x, & x\ge 3\end{aligned}
$$

Earlier part 1:

It is known that $f$ is continuous at $x=1.$ Find the value of $a.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $a=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $e+1$

Earlier part 2:

${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{x}^{3}+2}{f(x)}=$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        $\frac{3}{e+2}$

Current part:

Consider the part of $f(x)$ that's defined on the interval $x\in [3,c],$ where $c>3.$ Calculate the value of $c$ such that the average rate of change over $[3,c]$ is equal to $6.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $c=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Over the interval $x\in [3,c],$ we use the expression $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x.$

Let's calculate the average rate of change of $f(x)$ over the interval $[3,c]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(c)-f(3)}{c-3} \\  & =\frac{({c}^{2}-2c)-({3}^{2}-2\cdot 3)}{c-3} \\  & =\frac{{c}^{2}-2c-3}{c-3} \\  & =\frac{(c-3)(c+1)}{c-3} \\  & =c+1\end{aligned}
$$

We want this average rate of change to be equal to $6.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =6 \\ c+1 & =6 \\ c & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's compute the step size $Δx,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our integral are $a=4$ and $b=7,$ and there are $n=3$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{7-4}{3}=1.
$$

Now, let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059980/assets/18d2d2d79746d5782d27769b644b31f36c76fc7cf9d867788490d74935439b4e.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(4)+f(5)+f(6)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $4$ | $8$ |
| $5$ | $15$ |
| $6$ | $24$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(8+15+24)\cdot 1 \\  & =47\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ and the $x$-axis between $x=4$ and $x=7$ as the following definite integral:

$$
A={\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x
$$

This definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

	

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

In the definite integral above, the function is $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x,$ the lower bound is $a=4,$ and the upper bound is $b=7.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{7-4}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{7}({x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(4+\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{(4+\frac{3k}{n})}^{2}-2(4+\frac{3k}{n})]\cdot \frac{3}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$
